title: One man for the people (John 11:45–57)
hook: the council plots; Caiaphas says it's better one man die

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus wept at a tomb, then called Lazarus out, still wrapped in grave clothes. Your line was loose him, let him go. What did you help unwrap? Day six hundred twenty-four.

A room, worried people, and someone saying the hard, practical thing out loud. That's today's scene. After Lazarus walks out of the tomb, many who saw it believe. Some go to Jerusalem and report what happened. And the chief priests and leaders call an emergency meeting of the council. Their question is a frightened one, and very human: "What do we? for this man doeth many miracles." They're not debating whether the miracle happened. They're asking what it will cost them.

To understand the room, you have to understand the pressure on it. Judea was under Roman occupation. Rome let the temple and its leaders keep a measure of authority, as long as there was order. Crowds, excitement, talk of a king: that was exactly what Rome crushed. The council says it plainly: "If we let him thus alone, all men will believe on him: and the Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation." Their fear wasn't imaginary. Decades later, Roman armies did destroy the temple. Then the high priest that year, Caiaphas, speaks. "Ye know nothing at all, nor consider that it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation perish not." Expedient means better, useful, the practical choice. One life traded for many. It's an old logic: sacrifice one to keep the peace. And then John does something remarkable. He says Caiaphas spoke better than he knew. Being high priest, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation, "and not for that nation only, but that also he should gather together in one the children of God that were scattered abroad." The same sentence, heard two ways. Caiaphas meant politics. John hears the gospel in it: one man dying for the people, gathering the scattered. From that day, John says, they made plans. Jesus withdraws to a town called Ephraim, near the wilderness. Passover is near, and the whole city is wondering: will he come to the feast? It was Rome that would carry out the execution. But the road toward it begins in a frightened room.
screen: then, large: `ONE MAN SHOULD DIE FOR THE PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold leaders under pressure in mind. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who makes hard decisions for others. A mayor, a head of state, a school principal, a hospital director, a manager at work. Imagine the weight of their room: competing fears, real dangers, people who'll be hurt either way. You don't have to agree with them. Just picture them as people under pressure. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, for wisdom and courage, and that no one is sacrificed for convenience. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with honesty and fairness. The bell holds the time.
Caiaphas. The high priest who said one man should die for the people, which John hears as an unknowing prophecy of Jesus's death.
Your line: for the nation. Today, when you hear news about a leader's hard decision, pause and ask who pays the price for it. Day six hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Many churches pray for those in authority in their regular services; Christians read Caiaphas's words as an unknowing prophecy that Jesus would die for many.

fork.setup: you're on the council. crowds are following a miracle worker, and Rome is watching. what does Caiaphas propose?
options: invite him to address the council.
let one man die so the whole nation doesn't perish.
do nothing and see what happens.
fork.reveal: "it is expedient for us, that one man should die for the people." John hears in it more than Caiaphas meant.

original.note: Greek: it is better, it's to our advantage. The King James says expedient.

trapdoor: what you thought: the religious leaders simply hated Jesus.
what it means: a frightened council under Roman occupation makes a practical, terrible choice: one life to protect the many.
what a scholar hears: John reads Caiaphas's words as unknowing prophecy, given, John says, because he was high priest that year.

notes: KJV 11:49–50 capitalizes 'Nor' (start of verse 50); voice uses lowercase 'nor' mid-sentence. Confirm acceptable.
Caiaphas's tenure c. AD 18–36; the 'Caiaphas ossuary' found in Jerusalem in 1990 (identification debated). Confirm trapdoor.
The script frames the council under Roman pressure, and states that Rome carried out the execution, per the style guide. Confirm.
Destruction of the temple in AD 70. Confirm.
